label: Real run on this Mac's Docker Compose stack, with synthetic traffic from klaxon.traffic: synthetic data, a simulated provider, no real money. One fault from klaxon.faults, provider-outage, was injected on purpose. The alert was raised by klaxon.alerts from what the stack showed. Klaxon's loop ran live on it, through Claude Code on Aravind's seat, and stopped on diagnosed after 8 steps; any reply it got is a recorded response, not a simulation. It was offered one write action (rollback_deploy), as in week 4; in an evaluation run its gate only plans an action the diagnosis names: nobody is asked, and nothing runs. The diagnosis was compared with the fault's recorded cause by a rule (klaxon.grading), not by a person or a model. Its diagnosis named no action, so nobody was asked to approve one. The fault's cause was removed by the harness's clearing: this fault's cause is not a deploy.

case.name: provider-outage
case.title: Payments fail: the provider hangs, and our circuit breaker fails fast
case.right_answer: The fault's recorded cause: the provider's charge and refund API hangs (5 s, then 503): our payments API's calls to it time out, each after 3 attempts, until its circuit breaker opens, after 5 calls in a row got no answer; from then on it fails fast, answering 503 'outcome unknown' at once without calling the provider, and lets one trial call through 10 s after it opened, and again after each trial that fails.
case.remedy: nothing to change on our side: the provider must recover (escalate to it). Meanwhile the circuit breaker keeps the API answering at once, and closes again when a trial call gets an answer. After it recovers, the payments and refunds left pending need a decision (retry them with their keys, or mark them failed): a refund left pending blocks new refunds on its payment until it settles

diagnosis.hypothesis: fake-provider (the outside payment provider) degraded from about 07:15 to 07:17. It answered some POST /v1/payments calls with 500 and left others hanging until payments-api's 3 s read timeout. Each request retried three times, which gives the 9.6 s traces and the p95 latency alert. The PROVIDER_BREAKER then opened. From about 07:16:52 payments-api stopped calling the provider and answered 503 straight away, with the payment left pending. That produced the 96% 5xx rate. The cause is on the provider side, not in our services. The container is healthy with no restarts, and every service was created together at 07:15:05, so no deploy or setting change stands out. The evidence does not show why the provider is slow or failing. Rising load is one possibility; I did not check it. Because payments were left pending, some may have been created at the provider despite the timeouts, so the money check should be run after recovery.

evidence.shows: 503s on payments-api rose from about 0.1/s to 3.96/s at 07:16:52 and 11.5/s at 07:17:22, while 201s collapsed from 3.5/s to 0.3/s.
Error logs say '/v1/payments not sent: the circuit breaker is open' and 'provider unavailable; payment left pending'. The 503s are the breaker rejecting calls locally.
Before the breaker opened, calls to the provider had a mix of 500 responses (up to about 0.4/s) and 200s. Both fell to 0 by 07:17 once calls stopped.
Slow POST /payments traces of 3.2 to 9.6 s started at about 07:16:32, shortly before the 503 surge.
In the 9.6 s trace, three consecutive POSTs to fake-provider /v1/payments each ended in httpx.ReadTimeout after about 3 s. The Postgres and Redis spans took under 0.4 ms.
All containers, including fake-provider and payments-api, are running and healthy with 0 restarts, so the failure is not a crash.
All containers were created at 07:15:05 with the same image and no differing settings. PROVIDER_BREAKER is on, as designed, and no single deploy points to a cause.

proposed_fix.target: fake-provider (external provider) and payments-api circuit breaker
proposed_fix.summary: No listed action fixes this: a rollback of payments-api would not restore the provider. Check the provider's status or contact its owner. The breaker will recover by itself through trial calls once the provider answers. Afterwards, run money_check and reconcile the payments left pending, which may or may not exist at the provider.

diagnosis.blast_radius: No change is proposed, so nothing is affected. Until the provider recovers, new payments keep failing with 503 and stay pending. A rollback of payments-api would add a restart pause without addressing the cause.
diagnosis.rollback_plan: Not applicable, since no change is made. If the provider is later restarted or reconfigured, undo that through the provider owner and keep the breaker on.
